title: Adding a second route to a portfolio that never had one
excerpt: My portfolio was a single scrolling page with a scroll-spy sidebar. Adding a blog meant introducing real routing without breaking navigation that had no idea routes existed.
content: My portfolio started as one page. Ten sections stacked in a single scroll column, a fixed sidebar, and an `IntersectionObserver` deciding which nav item was active. No router, no pages — just anchors and scroll position. That worked until I wanted a blog. ## The problem with anchors Every sidebar link looked like this: ```jsx {item.label} ``` On a single page that is genuinely the right answer. It costs nothing, it survives a refresh, and the browser handles smooth scrolling for free. The active state came from a scroll-spy hook watching all ten sections at once: ```js const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => { entries.forEach((entry) => { if (entry.isIntersecting) visible.set(entry.target.id, entry.boundingClientRect.top); else visible.delete(entry.target.id); }); // the section closest to the top wins }); ``` The moment `/blog` exists, both assumptions break. `#about` means nothing on `/blog` — there is no `#about` element on that page to scroll to. And the scroll-spy has no sections to observe, so `activeId` falls back to whatever the first item is, leaving "Dashboard" highlighted while you read an article. ## What I did instead I gave nav items two possible shapes in the same registry: ```js { id: "about", label: "About", icon: User } // anchor on "/" { to: "/blog", label: "Blog", icon: Newspaper } // real route ``` Then the link component branches once: - An item with `to` renders a router `Link` and is active when the path matches. - An item with `id` renders an anchor. On `/` it stays `#about`. Anywhere else it becomes `/#about`, so clicking it navigates home *and* lands on the right section. That last detail is the one I would have missed if I hadn't clicked every link. `href="#about"` from `/blog/some-post` doesn't navigate anywhere — it just sets a fragment on a URL with no matching element, and nothing happens. Silent, not broken-looking, which is worse. ## Scroll-spy needs an off switch The other half is telling the spy to stand down when there is nothing to spy on: ```js const isHome = pathname === "/"; const activeSection = useActiveSection(isHome ? sectionIds : []); const activeId = isHome ? activeSection : routeIdFor(pathname); ``` The hook already bailed out when it found no elements, so passing an empty list was enough — no changes to the hook itself. Small mercy. ## Why not hash routes I considered `#/blog/some-post` to avoid touching server config. It needs zero deployment changes and works on any static host. I skipped it because of what the blog is *for*. An article URL gets pasted into a chat, a tweet, a search result. `#/blog/post` is invisible to crawlers as a distinct page — everything after the `#` never reaches the server, so every article shares one URL as far as any indexer is concerned. That defeats the point of writing them. Real paths mean one rewrite rule so a refresh on a deep link doesn't 404: ```json { "rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }] } ``` One file, and the URLs are honest. ## What I'd tell myself earlier The integration cost of a router isn't installing it. It's every component that quietly assumed there was only one page — in my case a nav registry, a scroll-spy hook, and the mental model that "active section" and "active page" are the same thing. They aren't, and separating them took longer than adding the routes.
author: Leomar Abad
